# Rental Scam Detector

Paste a rental listing URL. The tool reads the advert, reverse image searches
every photograph with [Zenserp](https://zenserp.com), and tells you where else
those exact pictures already appear.

Rental fraud almost always starts the same way: someone lifts the photographs
from a genuine advert and reposts the property cheaper. Finding those photos on
another site is the clearest signal available — and the same check catches the
honest case too, where a real property was listed elsewhere first and has
probably already gone.

Built with **Zenserp**, an [APILayer](https://apilayer.com/) product.

## How it grades

Finding the same photographs on another site is **not** evidence of anything on
its own. Letting agents cross-post the same property to every portal going. What
the tool actually weighs is whether the details on those other pages agree.

| Signal | Weight | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same photos, price differs by 35%+ | up to 50 | Two adverts for the same rooms at very different rents. One of them is lying |
| Same photos, different location | up to 50 | The same rooms advertised somewhere else entirely |
| Payment demanded before viewing | 20 | Defining move of advance-fee fraud |
| Untraceable payment method | 18 | Wire transfer, crypto, gift cards |
| Landlord claims to be abroad | 16 | Explains away the missing viewing |
| Viewing refused | 16 | No legitimate landlord refuses |
| Keys to be posted | 14 | Follows the "abroad" story |
| Free email as contact | 8 | Agencies use their own domain |
| Manufactured urgency | 6 | Pressure to pay before thinking |

When the photos turn up elsewhere but the price and place agree, that is
reported as a normal cross-post and scores nothing. It still answers the other
question this tool is for: the property is advertised widely and may already be
gone.

Every finding is listed with the evidence behind it and what it contributed, and
each matching page carries its own reasons, so the verdict can be argued with
rather than taken on faith.

A hit on the listing's **own** domain is expected and ignored. Only matches on
other hosts count.

### Comparing rents honestly

Weekly and monthly adverts are both common, so every figure is converted to a
monthly equivalent before anything is compared. `£340/wk` against `£1,400 pcm`
is a 5% difference, not a 75% one.

Where a period is missing the comparison is refused rather than guessed. A bare
`£325` next to `£340/wk` is almost certainly also weekly; treating it as monthly
would manufacture a 78% discount and invent exactly the red flag this tool is
supposed to find honestly.

## Running it

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Create `.env.local` from `.env.example`:

```bash
ZENSERP_API_KEY=        # https://app.zenserp.com/register
ZENSERP_TIMEOUT_MS=     # optional, default 90000
```

## Things worth knowing

- **A reverse image lookup takes ~30–60 seconds.** Zenserp drives a real search
  engine behind the scenes. Measured latency on the same image varied between 28s
  and 53s. Searches run concurrently, so the whole analysis is roughly as slow as
  the slowest single photo rather than the sum — but it is still a slow request,
  and the UI narrates the wait instead of hiding it.
- **`maxDuration` is set to 120s** on the route. Hosts that honour it (Vercel)
  will allow the full analysis; a 10-second serverless ceiling will cut it off.
- **Only the first four photographs are searched.** One Zenserp call per photo
  is the expensive part, galleries repeat the same rooms, and a scammer who
  lifted one picture lifted the set. Images are ranked before selection —
  structured data and Open Graph first, then page markup — so the four searched
  are the actual listing photos, not interface furniture.
- **Some portals block automated requests.** A 403 is reported plainly rather
  than being passed off as a clean result.
- **A clean result is not a guarantee.** It means nothing surfaced, not that the
  listing is safe. Always view a property in person before paying anything.

# Rental Scam Detector - check a listing before you pay a deposit

> A free tool that reverse image searches every photograph in a rental listing
> and shows you every other page using those same pictures, along with whether
> the price, the address or the dates changed between postings. Powered by the
> Zenserp API from APILayer.

## What it answers

- **Is this rental listing a scam?** Paste the link. The tool reads the advert,
  collects the photographs and searches each one across the web.
- **Where else do these photos appear?** Every matching page is listed with its
  price, location and date, so you can compare them yourself.
- **Is cross-posting suspicious?** No. Letting agents list the same property on
  several portals at once. What matters is whether the details changed.
- **Why is a much lower price a warning?** Deposit fraud works by making the
  property irresistible. If the same rooms are at market rate elsewhere, the
  cheap listing is usually the fake one.
- **The portal blocked the tool. What now?** Upload the photographs directly
  with the page they came from, or use the browser extension, which reads the
  listing you are already viewing.

## How it works

The listing page is fetched and parsed for photographs. Each photograph is sent
to Zenserp's reverse image search, which is driven by Google Lens, and the
results are grouped per image. For every page found carrying the same picture,
the asking price, stated location and listing date are compared against the
original. Prices are only compared when the periods match, so a weekly rate is
never measured against a monthly one.

## Limits

- Finding the same photographs elsewhere is not proof of fraud on its own.
- A listing with original photographs and no matches can still be a scam.
- Some portals return 403 to automated requests; use the extension for those.
- Never pay a deposit for a property you have not seen in person, and treat
  pressure to transfer money quickly as the warning sign it is.

## Data source

Zenserp (https://zenserp.com), an APILayer product. Free tier available.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I know if a rental listing is a scam?

The strongest signal is the photographs. Scammers rarely take their own, so they lift them from a real advert somewhere else. This tool reverse image searches every photo on the listing and shows you every other page using those same pictures. Finding the property elsewhere is not proof of anything on its own, because agents cross-post constantly. What matters is whether the price, the address or the contact details changed between postings.

### Is cross-posting the same as a scam?

No, and treating it that way is the most common mistake. Letting agents list the same property on several portals at once, which is normal and expected. A listing appearing in five places is unremarkable. The same rooms advertised at half the price, in a different city, or by a different person is what a scam looks like.

### What does the tool actually check?

It reads the advert, extracts the photographs, and reverse image searches each one through Zenserp, which is driven by Google Lens. For every other page using those images it compares the asking price, the stated location and the listing date against the one you gave it. You get the reasons alongside the links, so you can judge the evidence yourself rather than trusting a score.

### Why does a cheaper price mean something is wrong?

A deposit scam works by making the property irresistible. If the same rooms are advertised elsewhere at the market rate and the listing in front of you is far below it, the cheap one is usually the fake. The tool only compares prices that are genuinely comparable, so a weekly rate is never measured against a monthly one.

### The site blocked the tool. What now?

Some portals refuse automated requests outright and return a 403. When that happens you have two options: upload the photographs directly along with the page they came from, or install the browser extension, which reads the listing you are already looking at so the portal sees an ordinary visit.

### What is Zenserp?

Zenserp is a search engine results API from APILayer. It returns Google, Bing and Google Lens results as structured JSON, including reverse image search, which is what this tool uses to find every other page carrying a listing's photographs.

### Does this guarantee a listing is safe?

No. It finds a specific and very common kind of fraud, the kind that reuses photographs from a genuine advert. A listing with original photographs and no matches elsewhere can still be a scam. Never pay a deposit for a property you have not seen, never send money by bank transfer to someone you have not met, and treat pressure to pay quickly as the warning it is.

## Links

- Tool: https://apilayer.com/devtools/rental-scam-detector
- Zenserp API: https://zenserp.com
- APILayer: https://apilayer.com
